docs.title: Countersign
docs.text:
A remote job can authenticate to an mTLS site using a client certificate on your desktop. You approve a particular certificate, host and duration. The desktop signs each new handshake through the operating system’s key provider. The Integrator runs the Gateway that carries the job’s traffic.

Run the demo and verify a certificate fingerprint

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
Your task Guide Decide whether to approve a request or end access Use the Companion Give a job access on behalf of a signed-in user Integrate a service Configure protected hosts, run the services, or recover a Broker Self-host and operate Trace the two TLS connections and the signing request Architecture and trust Find a supported combination of OS, architecture and provider Tested platforms Build the app or reproduce a qualification run Develop and release

Looking up a field? See the configuration reference, Broker API, widget and theme manifest, or control protocol.

docs.title: Architecture and trust
docs.text:
The Gateway is the TLS client the protected site sees. The user's desktop supplies the client-certificate signature for that handshake. The Gateway holds traffic keys for both connections and sees the job's HTTP requests and responses. Trust the Integrator that operates it with anything the job can read or send under the grant.

Solid arrows show the application's traffic. Dashed arrows show control connections and local signing. Every Integrator runs its own Broker and Gateway. A single Companion can maintain outbound connections to multiple paired Brokers. Trace the first protected request

docs.title: Follow a request across the two connections
docs.text:
1. Workload → Gateway. curl, Python or another HTTPS client asks its configured proxy to CONNECT to a DNS name and port. The Gateway checks the protected destination and Workload binding with the Broker. For an admitted grant, its worker presents a fresh leaf for the exact intercepted host. The Workload validates this leaf against the proxy CA the Integrator supplied.
  2. Gateway → protected site. The Gateway opens a separate connection to the pinned destination. It authenticates the upstream server under that destination's trust policy. When the server requests client authentication, rustls asks for a signature over the TLS handshake input.
  3. Gateway → Broker → Companion. The Broker checks the live grant and signing operation, then routes the request to the desktop that approved it. The Companion verifies its local approval and invokes the native key provider. The selected public certificate chain and the resulting signature let the Gateway finish the handshake. The client private key stays in its provider.
  4. Site → Workload. The site authenticates the client's certificate and applies its own application permissions. The worker relays the response over the downstream TLS connection. The Broker handles authorization and signing messages. Application bodies travel through the Gateway.

docs.title: Who holds what
docs.text:
Component What it holds or sees What you trust it to do Integrator backend Authenticated account, Context ownership, job generation, service credential Bind each job to the correct user and Context, authorize its destinations, deliver credentials privately. Workload Job data, proxy address, public trust bundle. In shared mode it or its private adapter also has a Workload credential. Use the configured proxy. The Integrator controls direct network access from the job. Gateway Downstream and upstream traffic keys, plaintext, scoped signing requests. The parent holds issuer access. Enforce exact authorities, isolate grants, authenticate the upstream site and close both sockets when authority lapses. A compromised Gateway could send other requests to an approved site. Broker Pairings, account bindings, decisions, selected public chain, grants, audit and current signing operations Authenticate both services and devices, enforce ownership and deadlines, and send a signing request only to its winning device. Companion and native provider Device pairing key and access to installed client identities Display the actual origin and scope, require consent, and sign with the approved local key. Trust also extends to the user's OS, token provider and desktop session. Protected site Client certificate and the HTTP request it receives Decide what that certificate can do. The site may issue its own cookies or persist writes beyond the TLS session.

The widget lives on the Integrator's site. An OS notification, a deep link or Web Push carries an opaque ID. The Companion fetches the corresponding request on its authenticated connection. Branding comes from the accepted manifest for that pairing. The Integrator cannot supply the approval controls or substitute a different verified origin.

docs.title: The sidecar CA shares a host with the job
docs.text:
A new sidecar creates its CA key in memory. It writes the public certificate to the volume the Workload reads. The Gateway and Workload need separate process and filesystem permissions. A privileged job that can inspect the Gateway process, trace it, or control the container runtime can defeat that boundary. The Compose demonstration tests isolation from inside the Workload. Sidecar process boundaries and operating requirements

The CA has a critical DNS name constraint for each permitted suffix and excludes all IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. For *.team.example:443 the encoded DNS constraint is team.example. X.509 permits the apex and subdomains under that suffix. Gateway policy is narrower: it matches one additional label, checks the port and resolves exact-host overrides. Every issued leaf names one exact host. Clients are responsible for validating their trust store and certificate constraints. Restart the sidecar with a new CA when its destination policy changes.

In shared mode the supervisor uses a local issuing key or an ACM-PCA-compatible issuer and authenticates the connecting Workload. In both modes a Linux worker is assigned to one grant. Streams, sockets, TLS sessions and certificate selection cannot move into another user's grant, including when two users contact the same host. Shared Gateway operation

docs.title: When access ends
docs.text:
An approval duration bounds how long the job may use the selected identity. A lease is a shorter permission the traffic and signing relays need to keep working. The Broker checks current authority on renewal. Traffic leases have a maximum budget of 30 seconds, measured conservatively from when the enforcer sent the request. The Gateway attempts renewal about every ten seconds. An earlier grant, certificate or validation deadline wins, including for an idle connection.

An offline Companion can queue a revocation. The cutoff guarantee starts when the Broker records it. A retirement notice can close the sockets sooner. Lost notices, a stalled worker or an unreachable Broker cannot extend an issued lease. The Integrator can check the recorded decision and any reported socket closures separately. Bytes a site has already received, sessions it established independently and changes it already committed remain subject to that site's own controls. Status and observations

The name “countersign” also appears in COSE for a signature over another secured message. This project delegates the TLS client-authentication signature in an ordinary mTLS handshake.

docs.title: Use the Companion
docs.text: Install the Companion on the computer that already holds your client certificate. Your remote job can then ask this computer to authenticate to a website. Pair each Integrator once. When a request arrives, you decide which certificate the job may use, where it may use it and for how long.

docs.title: Install the Companion
docs.text:
Choose the desktop artifact for your operating system and processor from the distribution run. Each archive contains the installer and a separate native addon for developers. The installer already includes its matching addon. These builds are unsigned. Installer artifacts · Tested platforms

Desktop Package Where the Companion finds your website certificate Windows Run the per-user .exe installer and open Countersign from Start. The current user's Personal certificate store, backed by a CNG signing key. macOS Open the .pkg installer, then open Countersign from Applications. A Keychain identity whose private key is accessible to Security.framework. Linux Install the .deb with your package manager, or make the .AppImage executable and launch it in your desktop session. A PKCS#11 token available through p11-kit or the configured module. Unlock your encrypted login keyring before pairing.

Enable Start at login under Settings if this computer should receive requests after sign-in. Open the window again from the tray using Open Countersign. Linux users can also build and install the local conda package.

docs.title: Find your way around
docs.text:
The window has three tabs. Requests shows one approval request at a time and opens by itself when a request arrives. Integrators lists your pairings, each with its own details page. Settings holds Start at login. The window follows your system's light or dark appearance.

While a request, a pairing confirmation or an Integrator's details are on screen, the whole window takes on that Integrator's colours, with its logo, name and copy in the header beside its verified origin. Lists, Settings and Integrators that publish no branding use Countersign's purple theme. Whatever the colours, the Companion draws the request facts, warnings, certificate details and the Deny and Approve buttons the same way, and the countersign mark stays at the bottom right. What a theme can change

docs.title: Pair an Integrator
docs.text:
1. Get the Integrator's HTTPS origin from your signed-in service. On the Integrators tab, enter the full origin, including a nonstandard port, in Integrator origin and choose Pair.
  2. The Companion opens the Integrator in your browser and shows a pairing code. Sign into the intended account in the browser and enter that code.
  3. Back in the Companion, check the verified origin, account and code before choosing Confirm pairing. The Integrator then appears in the list. A second Integrator gets its own pairing and connection.

The browser half of pairing is illustrated in the demo walkthrough.

docs.title: Decide what to approve
docs.text:
Open the local notification, choose Open Companion on the Integrator's site, or open the tray app. Requests wait in a queue and the Companion shows the oldest first, with a count of the others. Read the verified origin and account first under Checked by Countersign, then check that the Context corresponds to the job you started. Requested host identifies the immediate connection. Approval covers describes every destination the job can reach with this grant.

The Companion lists the eligible installed certificates. With two or more, you must select one before Approve becomes available. When certificates share a name, the part of each SHA-256 fingerprint where they first differ is highlighted, and a pattern drawn from the fingerprint sits beside each one. Also compare the issuer and expiry. With one eligible certificate, it is selected and still needs your approval. If none qualify, or the certificate provider is unavailable, a warning explains why and you can deny the request. Only the selected public chain is sent to the Broker.

Pick 15 min, 1 h or 8 h, or choose Custom to enter minutes. The administrator's limit disables longer presets. Access ends shows the time the approval stops and how far away it is. If the selected certificate expires first, a warning says that access ends with the certificate. Approval lets this job use the certificate for further handshakes within that scope and duration. A native provider may separately prompt to unlock a key or token.

Each request that appears locks Approve for about a second, so a click meant for the previous screen cannot approve it. When the next request comes from a different Integrator, a banner reads Now showing a request from and the origin, and the window changes to that Integrator's colours.

docs.title: Read a wildcard approval
docs.text:
In this example, the job requested reports.team.example:9444. The administrator enabled approval for the whole *.team.example:9444 entry. That can also cover archive.team.example:9444 under the same policy. The apex, deeper names and other ports fall outside this scope. The normal setting even for a wildcard entry is an approval for the single requested host.

Choose Deny if the scope is wider than you intended. The Integrator can request access again after it changes the policy. If several desktops receive an offer, the first committed decision settles it for all of them. An approved grant uses the identity on the desktop that won the request.

docs.title: Manage an Integrator
docs.text:
Choose an Integrator on the Integrators tab to open its details. The page shows the connection status, current approvals, the Companions paired to your account, and any security notices. This computer marks this Companion's own pairing in the device list.

Action What happens Close the window The Companion stays in the tray and continues to receive requests and sign approved handshakes. Choose Quit in the tray New handshakes require the approving desktop to reconnect. Established traffic can continue while its leases renew, up to the grant's expiry. Choose Revoke access on an approval The Companion queues the revocation and shows when the Broker records it. From that point outstanding traffic has at most its existing lease budget. Choose Remove from this computer After you confirm in the dialog, deletes this computer's pairing key and local state. Use the Integrator's device controls to end the remote pairing and grants. Choose Revoke pairing at Integrator After you confirm, opens the verified Integrator's device-management page. Select the pairing to forget. You can also use that page from another computer if this one is lost.

If another Companion connects to your account, a notice gives its connection information and device ID. Review the ID before choosing Disconnect device or Disconnect all other devices, and confirm in the dialog. Removing another device revokes its grants. An independent lease deadline bounds the remaining traffic. How revocation works

docs.title: Review a branding change
docs.text: If a paired Integrator changes its logo, name, copy or colours, its details page shows the current and proposed branding side by side. Choose Accept new branding to adopt it, which also changes the colours the window takes on for that Integrator. Choose Keep current to dismiss it. The Companion does not ask again about the same proposal, only about a later change. The verified origin and approval controls belong to the Companion either way.

docs.title: When an approval doesn't work
docs.text: What you see What to check No desktop notification Open the Requests tab, then check the Integrator's status on the Integrators tab. A web notification or deep link locates a pending request. It cannot approve one. No eligible installed certificate Check that the identity is valid for client authentication, has its private key, and matches the issuer and signature schemes allowed for this destination. Ask the Integrator which identity it expects. Provider unavailable Unlock the native provider and reconnect the token if applicable. On Linux verify that p11-kit can see the token in the same login session. Request access again. Approved, but the job still cannot connect Look for Ready for handshakes in the Integrator's details on the approving desktop. If the original connection attempt timed out, retry it from the job. The Integrator can distinguish an approval from an accepted upstream handshake. Revocation queued Reconnect to the verified Integrator and use Retry revocation. If the desktop cannot reconnect, revoke through the Integrator. The lease cutoff starts from the Broker's recorded decision.

docs.title: Install from npm
docs.text: Run npx @zeroae/countersign on the desktop. npm downloads the platform package for your Node architecture (x64 or ARM64). The command opens the installer on Windows and macOS, or runs the AppImage on Linux. To locate the file for manual installation, run npx @zeroae/countersign --print-path. The binary ships inside the npm tarball.

docs.title: Develop and release
docs.text: The Cargo workspace contains the protocol, PKI validation, Broker, Gateway and native addon. The pnpm workspace contains the Electron Companion, web widget and demo Integrator. Use the Rust toolchain pinned in rust-toolchain.toml, Node 24 and pnpm 10.28.2. On Ubuntu install libnss3-dev for native builds and bubblewrap for Gateway runtime tests.

docs.title: Build the Companion
docs.text:
From the checkout root, run the following on the same OS and architecture as the Electron executable you intend to use.

pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
cargo build --locked -p countersign-native
node scripts/native-package.mjs debug
pnpm --filter @countersign/companion exec electron-builder --dir --publish never

The staging script copies the host's production addon and checks its exported functions. The unpacked app is under packages/companion/dist/. On Linux, the executable is linux-unpacked/countersign-companion on x64 or linux-arm64-unpacked/countersign-companion on ARM64. Pass that executable to the demo launcher. To produce the host's installer, build the crate with --release, run node scripts/native-package.mjs, then run pnpm --filter @countersign/companion package.

docs.title: Run the checks
docs.text:
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace --locked
pnpm lint
pnpm test

docs.title: The pre-commit hook
docs.text:
A tracked pre-commit hook, .githooks/pre-commit, runs fast checks on what you stage. It refuses a commit when a staged Rust file is not formatted as cargo fmt would format it, and when a staged JavaScript file that pnpm lint covers fails ESLint: the packages' src and test folders and the demo Integrator. It checks the staged copy of each file, not the one in your working tree. When node_modules is missing it skips ESLint and says so. It finishes in well under a second. It runs no build, no test suite and no network call. Clippy, the test suites and the Gateway's runtime test run in the CI workflow and the end-to-end workflow.

A Claude session installs the hook when it starts, through the SessionStart hook in .claude/settings.json. Without Claude, install it once per clone from the checkout root:

scripts/install-git-hooks.sh

The script sets core.hooksPath to .githooks. That setting covers every worktree of the clone, and each worktree runs its own tracked copy of the hook. If core.hooksPath already points elsewhere, or the clone's .git/hooks folder holds hooks of its own, which core.hooksPath would stop running, the script changes nothing and says so. To skip the hook for one commit, run git commit --no-verify. The tests for the hook and the script are in scripts/test_git_hooks.py:

python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts -p 'test_git_hooks.py'

To run the Gateway's tests under the filter sandbox on a host that refuses namespaces, run scripts/filter-sandbox-container.sh, which needs Docker. It runs the containment test and the runtime test in a container under Docker's default security profile, as the end-to-end workflow's gateway-filter-sandbox job does. Its two last steps use a profile with one quirk each: where the host refuses the allow-list, the filter sandbox has to fail at startup by name, and where the kernel has no close_range, a grant worker still has to start with no descriptor of the supervisor's.

That container has the CI runner's kernel. To run the same two tests on real ECS Fargate 1.4.0, x86-64 and arm64, use the qualification harness, qualification/fargate/run.sh. It needs our AWS account, and its README says how to deploy, run and tear it down. Run it for every release that touches the grant worker.

For the graphics and network path, run the demo walkthrough with --verify to automate the installed Companion and browser. The hosted end-to-end job also runs a separate harness that selects identities from candidate lists of different sizes, verifies the peer fingerprint and checks revocation. The native qualification jobs generate identities in disposable provider stores. On macOS and Windows use a disposable runner account for that harness because it changes user-level keychain or certificate-store state. End-to-end workflow · Native qualification workflow

docs.title: A grant worker died of SIGSYS
docs.text:
The worker sandbox's filter kills a grant worker with SIGSYS when it makes a system call outside the allow-list, or a listed call with an argument the list refuses. One call is the exception: clone3 fails as unsupported and kills nothing. The Gateway logs grant worker killed by the worker sandbox's filter (SIGSYS); grant fenced, which does not say which call it was. Two commands do.

The kernel writes an audit line for each filter kill, under either worker sandbox. Reading it needs no root where your user can read the system journal, as members of adm or systemd-journal can.

journalctl -k | grep type=1326

kernel: audit: type=1326 audit(1795144504.852:6342): ... pid=2188053 comm="worker_sandbox-" exe=".../target/debug/deps/worker_sandbox-dcf0f669f7f13f3c" sig=31 arch=c00000b7 syscall=56 compat=0 ip=0xec5e8e3f07c4 code=0x80000000

sig=31 is SIGSYS, syscall= is the number of the call and arch= the architecture that number belongs to: c000003e is x86-64 and c00000b7 is arm64. The line above is not a grant worker's. It comes from the containment test in crates/countersign-gateway/tests/worker_sandbox.rs, which has the filter kill a process on purpose many times in each run, and comm="worker_sandbox-" marks every such line. Leave those out: a grant worker's line names another comm and exe.

In CI the same lines come from sudo dmesg, which the CI and end-to-end workflows print when a run fails, in the step "Name the system call when the worker sandbox's filter killed a grant worker". A host that runs the audit daemon, auditd, sends these lines to /var/log/audit/audit.log and keeps them out of the journal.

When the number is not enough, trace the Gateway. The runtime test takes the Gateway executable as its argument, so give it a wrapper that starts the real one under strace. Besides strace, the test needs what its first lines list: bubblewrap, libnss-wrapper, curl and Python's cryptography. From the checkout root:

cat > /tmp/traced-gateway <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
exec strace -D -f -o "/tmp/gateway-trace.$$" "$PWD/target/debug/countersign-gateway" "$@"
EOF
chmod +x /tmp/traced-gateway
python3 crates/countersign-gateway/tests/runtime.py /tmp/traced-gateway

The wrapper runs strace -D -f -o <file> target/debug/countersign-gateway serve <config> for each Gateway the test starts, one trace file per Gateway. -f follows the Gateway into its grant workers. -D matters: the sidecar part of the runtime test stops every descendant of the process it started. Without -D that process is strace and the Gateway is its child, so the test stops the Gateway and hangs. With -D the Gateway is the process the test started, and the tracer runs outside its process tree. Tracing slows the Gateway, so one of the test's timing assertions can fail under it. The trace up to that point is still complete.

In each trace file, search for +++ killed by SIGSYS +++. A filter kill ends every thread of the grant worker, so the file has one such line for each thread, and for most of them the line above is an allowed call the thread was waiting in. Look in the lines before the first of them for the call the audit line named. The trace shows its arguments and what the grant worker did before it; ignore the result strace prints for it. The last Gateway the test starts has one grant worker the test itself kills, marked --- SIGSYS {si_signo=SIGSYS, si_code=SI_USER, ...} ---. That one is not a filter kill.

The same number is a different call on each architecture, so map it with the architecture from the audit line. ausyscall takes both:

ausyscall aarch64 56   # openat
ausyscall x86_64 56    # clone

ausyscall comes in the auditd package, and installing that starts the audit daemon, which takes the audit lines out of the journal as above. Without it, read the kernel's table for the architecture of the killed grant worker, which need not be the machine you are reading on: syscall_64.tbl for x86-64 and asm-generic/unistd.h for arm64. A host of the same architecture has it installed, as /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/asm/unistd_64.h on x86-64 and /usr/include/asm-generic/unistd.h on arm64, where grep -w 56 finds #define __NR_openat 56.

A call a grant worker needs goes in the allow-list in crates/countersign-gateway/src/worker_sandbox.rs, with the reason beside it as a comment: ALLOWED for a call allowed whatever its arguments, or conditional, in allow_list, for a call allowed only with certain arguments. When the killed call is already in conditional, an argument failed its test, and the trace shows which. A call a grant worker should not make is a bug in the grant worker, not a gap in the list.

docs.title: Install with conda on Linux
docs.text:
On a Linux desktop with rattler-build and conda installed, place the local channel outside the checkout. Build, install and start the packaged application in the graphical login session.

rattler-build build --recipe recipe/recipe.yaml --output-dir "$HOME/.cache/countersign-conda-output" -c conda-forge
conda create -n countersign-local -c "file://$HOME/.cache/countersign-conda-output" -c conda-forge countersign-companion
conda run -n countersign-local countersign-companion

The recipe installs Electron, the launcher and the matching native addon. A future conda-forge submission needs a versioned release source with its checksum. Recipe and package tests

docs.title: Preview and edit the handbook
docs.text:
Use Python 3.12 and the pinned documentation requirements.

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
.venv/bin/python -m mkdocs build --strict
.venv/bin/python -m mkdocs serve

The build writes a static site in site/. Version tags add a handbook snapshot to the gh-pages branch and deploy the archive to GitHub Pages. Use the version selector for an exact release. For example, /0.1.0/ stays at that release, /0.1/ follows stable patches in the 0.1 series, and /latest/ follows the newest stable release. Unversioned handbook links open the latest stable page. The documentation workflow runs the strict build on documentation PRs and attaches a countersign-handbook artifact. To read a downloaded artifact, extract it and run python3 -m http.server --bind 127.0.0.1 from the directory containing index.html.

Diagrams live in docs/assets/diagrams/, each with a light and a -dark variant. The architecture and deployment diagrams are hand-edited SVGs; the two sequence diagrams have Mermaid sources (.mmd). Every colour comes from palette.json. The hand-edited SVGs reference it only through var(--token), and the Mermaid sources and theme.json name tokens as {token}, for example rect {band-request}. The script stops on any other colour. Edit the light SVG or the .mmd source, then regenerate both variants from the checkout root. Mermaid export needs Node and a Chromium that Puppeteer can launch; set PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH to reuse an installed one.

python3 scripts/render_diagrams.py

The pages embed both variants with the #gh-light-mode-only and #gh-dark-mode-only suffixes, which GitHub and the handbook's theme toggle both honour. The original design and decision record remains available to contributors.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Screenshots are rendered, not captured by hand. scripts/capture_screenshots.mjs loads the real Companion renderer and the demo Integrator page in Playwright's Chromium. A stubbed window.countersign API and fixture /api responses supply the data, so no Broker, Gateway or certificate store is involved. The clock, locale and time zone are fixed, and every shot is taken at twice its CSS size. The demo page is captured in light and dark; the Companion has no dark theme yet. From the checkout root, after pnpm install:

pnpm exec playwright install chromium   # once
pnpm screenshots

The script writes raw captures and boxes.json, the CSS-pixel box of each highlighted element, to docs/assets/screenshots/raw/. scripts/annotate_screenshots.py, run by the same command, reads those boxes and draws the callouts onto the copies the pages embed. Change the fixtures or selectors in the capture script and the labels in the annotation script, then look at every changed image before committing. Set CHROMIUM_PATH or pass --browser to use another Chromium build, and --only widget,job-result to recapture a few shots. Every shot has a -dark twin, the Companion's included. Embed both with the #gh-light-mode-only and #gh-dark-mode-only suffixes, as for diagrams. The Companion shots render packages/companion/src with a stubbed window.countersign; extend the stub when the preload API changes. CI does not run the capture.

docs.title: What CI and release tags produce
docs.text:
Pushes run workspace and native checks on Linux and Windows. Pull requests and version releases also run macOS jobs. Distribution jobs on PRs build unsigned desktop installers, validate the bundled addon with Electron, and build the two container targets. See the tested platforms for the runs behind each claim.

Version tags matching v* trigger desktop builds, native prebuilds, GitHub release assets with SHA256SUMS, and the two GHCR images tagged with the release name. The image names are ghcr.io/zeroae/countersign-gateway and ghcr.io/zeroae/countersign-broker. Windows signing and macOS signing and notarization require the repository variable COUNTERSIGN_SIGN_RELEASES=true and the corresponding release secrets. A signed release still needs qualification on its intended operating systems. The conda recipe builds a local channel. Release workflow and required secrets

docs.title: Publish to crates.io and npm
docs.text: A version tag publishes the five Rust crates countersign-protocol, countersign-pki, countersign-native, countersign-broker and countersign-gateway, plus the browser package @zeroae/countersign-widget. All six carry the MIT License. Electron installers and native prebuilds remain GitHub release assets. Registry workflow

docs.title: Set up the first release
docs.text:
The GitHub environments crates.io and npm accept deployments from tags matching v*. Add each bootstrap credential under Settings → Environments in the named environment.

  1. Sign in to crates.io and verify your email. Create a short-lived API token with permission to publish new crates and new versions of the five crate names. Store it as CRATES_IO_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN in the GitHub crates.io environment. The first successful upload establishes ownership of each name. Cargo publishing guide
  2. Sign in to npm with an account authorized to create public packages in the @zeroae scope. For the first release, create a short-lived granular token with read/write access to packages in that scope and Bypass two-factor authentication enabled for CI. Save it as NPM_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN in the GitHub npm environment. npm access tokens

docs.title: Cut a release
docs.text:
Set the workspace version and internal dependency requirements in Cargo.toml and the version in packages/widget/package.json. Refresh and commit Cargo.lock with the version changes. From the reviewed commit, push the matching tag (for example, v0.1.0). The registry workflow checks that tag against every public package before either upload job starts. It builds the Rust archives, tests the widget and loads both exports from an installation of the npm tarball. Pull requests and release tags both run the Rust workspace tests on the release runner.

Cargo uploads dependencies before their consumers. npm publishes the tested tarball with provenance and uses latest for stable releases and next for prereleases such as v0.2.0-rc.1. If an upload fails, rerun the failed job on the same tag. Each registry job checks existing versions against the tested archives and skips matching uploads. A checksum conflict requires investigation before continuing.

If a failure requires a workflow fix after the release tag is public, merge the fix and push a tag named registry-retry/vX.Y.Z at the fixed commit. Permit that exact retry tag in both registry environments. The workflow fetches the original vX.Y.Z tag, pins the upload jobs to its commit, and checks that the workflow revision contains the same widget sources for npm provenance. Desktop and container distribution continues to use the original release tag.

docs.title: Switch to trusted publishing
docs.text:
After the first release, add a GitHub Actions trusted publisher in the settings of each crate and the npm widget. Use owner zeroae, repository countersign, workflow filename publish.yml, and the environment below.

Registry GitHub environment Publisher permissions crates.io crates.io Configure the publisher for each of the five crates. npm npm Allow direct npm publish for @zeroae/countersign-widget.

Delete the bootstrap secrets from GitHub and revoke both temporary tokens at their registries. Subsequent tags authenticate with the GitHub job's short-lived OIDC identity. Set up the npm publisher within two days of its first OIDC release, or recreate the configuration if it expires. crates.io trusted publishing · npm trusted publishing

The desktop distribution workflow packs the native installer on each of the six release runners and installs its npm archive into a clean consumer project. It checks the installed payload against the original binary. On a release, distribution.yml publishes the six @zeroae/countersign-{linux,darwin,win32}-{x64,arm64} packages before @zeroae/countersign. For trusted publishing, configure those seven npm packages with workflow filename distribution.yml and environment npm. The widget uses publish.yml.

docs.title: Add Countersign to a service
docs.text: Suppose an analyst starts a reconciliation job in your application. The job needs to read a statement from ledger.partner.example:443 using the analyst's client certificate. Treat the reconciliation as the Context, the job process as the Workload, and the analyst's existing application account as the owner. Your backend already knows who may start that job and which ledger it may contact.

docs.title: Put the integration on your origin
docs.text:
Run your own Broker and Gateway. Configure the same protected destination and policy version on both. Serve the widget on your authenticated application and expose the Broker's WebSocket upgrade at wss://portal.example/v1/companion on that same origin. The Companion will open /countersign/pair?attempt=… in the user's browser. Provide that page and an authenticated /countersign/devices page for managing a lost or retired pairing. The Broker backend and administrator routes are for your servers. Configuration · Broker API

  1. Offer a Pair Companion action that shows the HTTPS origin the analyst should enter in the installed Companion, here https://portal.example.
  2. When the analyst pairs, the Companion displays a code and opens your pairing page. Authenticate the analyst, show their account, and ask them to enter the code from the Companion. After they confirm, your backend checks the session, request Origin and CSRF token and posts the attempt, code and session-derived user ID to /v1/backend/pairings/confirm.
  3. The Companion shows the verified origin and account for a second confirmation. After the analyst confirms there, its protected pairing key signs a fresh challenge. The Broker records the pairing and the Companion shows Connected. The analyst can use the same Companion with another Integrator. Pairing and device controls

docs.title: Bind a job to its owner
docs.text:
The examples use Broker Integrator ID finance. Give every running instance an opaque ID. For example, user u-42 owns Context close-q3, and your scheduler assigned Workload export-981, generation 1. Bind those values on your backend when the job starts. Use a higher generation when replacing the instance.

The following Node example runs on the backend. brokerBase is your private HTTPS Broker origin and backendToken comes from your backend's secret store. The host's TLS client must trust the Broker's issuing CA.

async function brokerPost(path, body) {
  const response = await fetch(new URL("/v1/backend/" + path, brokerBase), {
    method: "POST",
    redirect: "error",
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000),
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      Authorization: "Bearer " + backendToken
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(body)
  });
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Broker returned HTTP " + response.status);
  return response.status === 204 ? null : response.json();
}

const job = {
  user: "u-42", context: "close-q3",
  workload: "export-981", workload_generation: 1
};
const issued = await brokerPost("workloads", { ...job, mode: "sidecar" });

Store issued.binding with the job. Configure the sidecar with that binding and deliver issued.token through a private credential file. Refresh the token for the same running generation before expires_at_ms and replace the file atomically. The demo refreshes every 60 seconds. Give the Workload the proxy settings and the sidecar's public CA certificate. Runnable sidecar demo · Token delivery in the demo backend

docs.title: Make the first protected request
docs.text:
From the job environment configured with HTTPS_PROXY and the sidecar's public CA bundle, run a normal HTTPS request.

curl --fail --show-error https://ledger.partner.example/statements/latest

With two or more eligible identities the analyst must select one before Approve becomes available. A wildcard destination normally prompts for the exact requested host. If the administrator enables whole-wildcard approval, the prompt shows both the initiating host and the broader scope. The certificate's private key stays on the analyst's machine. Companion approval screen

For an explicit Request access action, your authenticated page calls your backend. Resolve the job from the session and Context, then call the Broker with the stored binding and server-selected host.

const { id, state } = await brokerPost("requests", {
  binding: issued.binding,
  host: "ledger.partner.example:443"
});

Return the approval ID to the page. An explicit request joins a matching pending approval or returns its current approved record. After denial, cancellation or expiry, an explicit request starts a fresh approval. If the original CONNECT timed out, the Workload must deliberately issue another request after approval. Widget adapter and notification handlers

The widget draws only the pairing, request and launch controls in its own Countersign card. Your page explains the job, the pairing and what happens next. Restyle the widget

docs.title: Show progress and end access
docs.text:
Query status with the session-derived user ID and the approval ID. Show “Approved” for a committed decision, “Ready for handshakes” when ready is true, and “Upstream accepted mTLS” only after upstream_mtls_accepted is true. While the grant is active, expires_at_ms gives the deadline the user approved, so the page can count down to it. Closing the Companion can leave an existing leased connection usable until its authority expires. A fresh handshake needs the winning Companion online. Status fields and failure handling

Retire the Workload when the job exits. Close the Context when the reconciliation itself ends. To withdraw one grant earlier, revoke its approval ID. After a denial, expiry or revocation, say how access ended and offer a fresh request.

In the demo, the upstream requires a client certificate and returns the leaf fingerprint it actually received. Compare it with certificate.sha256, the certificate the user selected in the Companion. When the job's own connection started the approval, the backend finds it with approvals/current. Look it up as soon as the job's result lands and keep its ID, since a later renewal can make another approval current; the demo's Job result page does this. Demo upstream

docs.title: Operate a self-hosted Gateway and Broker
docs.text:
Run one Broker for the Integrator's HTTPS origin. Start with a sidecar for each Workload that needs its own proxy. Use shared mode when you can distribute a common proxy trust anchor, authenticate each Workload on an HTTPS listener and operate Linux worker isolation for multiple users. In both modes the Gateway sees HTTP plaintext and owns the traffic keys. The user's identity key stays with the native provider on their machine. Architecture · Configuration reference

To run the services from a checkout, build the two container targets from the repository root. The runnable demo wires the images to separate networks and volumes. Run the demo

docker build -f distribution/Dockerfile --target broker -t countersign-broker:local .
docker build -f distribution/Dockerfile --target gateway -t countersign-gateway:local .

docs.title: Choose the network and trust boundaries
docs.text: Each parent calls the Integrator's Broker over TLS. The Companion maintains its own outbound authenticated connection to that Broker. The parent retains the real downstream and upstream sockets. A worker receives connected local streams and creates the downstream leaf key. It negotiates both TLS legs and asks the Broker, through its parent, for a scoped client signature. The worker sandbox keeps each worker from files, the network, the supervisor and other workers. A new approval gets its own worker, including when the same user selects the same certificate for another Context.

docs.title: Sidecar
docs.text:
1. Put the Gateway and its one Workload on a private link. Bind listen only to the Workload-facing interface. Anyone who can connect to a sidecar listener can act as its Workload. In the Compose demo the upstream site shares the Gateway's backend network and cannot connect to its proxy port.
  2. Mount the Workload credential and configuration into the Gateway. Give the Gateway write access to a separate public trust directory. Mount that directory read-only at the same path in the Workload. Use separate principals and PID/mount namespaces, remove tracing privileges and keep the container engine socket outside the Workload. Protect the host's memory and swap according to the sensitivity of the traffic.
  3. Start countersign-gateway serve gateway.json. Startup probes an actual grant worker under the chosen worker sandbox and logs the sandbox and its layers. The sidecar creates a new CA and atomically publishes its public PEM at ca_output. Its CA key lives in parent memory until exit. The CA encodes critical DNS name constraints and excludes all IPv4 and IPv6 ranges. A wildcard constraint uses the bare DNS suffix, such as corp.example. The Gateway separately checks the exact port, label depth and apex policy. Client software is responsible for enforcing the constraint. The Gateway enforces destination policy and issues an exact-host leaf on every connection.
  4. Run countersign-gateway env gateway.json in the launcher and pass its exports to the Workload. Restrict direct egress if the job must use Countersign for a site. Check that the actual Workload UID can read the PEM and reach the proxy, and that it cannot read the private credential, Gateway memory or descriptors. The demo launcher performs these checks before sending curl traffic.

Keep the Linux supervisor unprivileged. With the default worker sandbox it requires /usr/bin/bwrap and permission to create user, mount, PID and network namespaces. On Ubuntu with restricted user namespaces the distribution supplies an opt-in bwrap-userns-restrict AppArmor profile in apparmor-profiles. Check both the host policy and the container's seccomp/AppArmor policy. The demo's container exceptions apply only to its Gateway. Compose deployment and access checks · Service mounts and networks

docs.title: Shared Gateway
docs.text:
Use shared.listener_cert and shared.listener_key for the HTTPS proxy listener. Configure the same independent Gateway service secret in the Gateway and Broker. The Workload or its private adapter presents a Gateway-audience bearer token on CONNECT. Give the Workload public trust for both the HTTPS proxy listener and the exact-host leaves the proxy will issue.

For example, an adapter can put one Proxy-Authorization: Bearer <workload-token> line in a private, short-lived header file for curl to read on the proxy hop.

curl --noproxy '' --proxy https://gateway.corp.example:8443 \
  --proxy-cacert /trust/listener-roots.pem \
  --proxy-header @/run/workload/proxy-headers \
  --cacert /trust/proxy-issuer.pem https://site.test:9444/

Choose a local issuing CA or an ACM-PCA-compatible service. For the local source, mount the issuer certificate chain and matching signing key only into the Gateway parent. For a remote source, let the parent obtain standard AWS SDK credentials. Grant issuance and retrieval for the intended authority and template. The issuer signs the worker's public CSR. The Gateway checks the resulting chain, public key, DNS SAN, server-auth usage and grant expiry before returning it to the worker. AWS Private CA and ZAE-ZCM use this same path. The configuration reference includes the standard profile and service endpoint settings. Shared CA configuration

Maintain affinity between a live grant and the Gateway supervisor that first admitted it. A replacement process has a fresh boot identity. Retire the old grant and obtain a fresh approval when moving its Workload. The two-user integration fixture exercises concurrent workers and cutoff on Linux. A production shared deployment, its confinement policy and a live issuing service need qualification in their target environment.

docs.title: Choose a worker sandbox
docs.text:
The Gateway runs each grant in its own grant worker, a short-lived process that holds that grant's traffic keys. The worker sandbox is the OS isolation around every grant worker. Set it with the Gateway field worker_sandbox. Both values work in sidecar and shared mode, and the supervisor stays unprivileged under both: neither needs the Gateway to run as root.

worker_sandbox Use it when What isolates a grant worker "namespaces" (default, recommended) The host lets an unprivileged process create user, mount, PID and network namespaces. The base layers, inside namespaces that bubblewrap creates: the grant worker has its own filesystem, process and network view. Requires /usr/bin/bwrap. "filter" The host refuses namespaces and you cannot change that, as on ECS Fargate. The base layers alone. Does not use bubblewrap.

Every grant worker applies the same base layers to itself before it reads any input:

  • a seccomp allow-list of the system calls a grant worker needs, which kills the grant worker on any other call. It cannot open a file, open a socket, run a program or signal another process;
  • Landlock, at the version the kernel offers, as a second refusal of file access, and of TCP and signals on newer kernels. A kernel without Landlock still starts, and the startup log says so;
  • non-dumpable memory, so no other process of the same user can read it;
  • no inherited environment, and no open descriptors beyond its control socket and standard streams.

Use the namespace sandbox wherever the host allows it. The filter sandbox gives up the namespace layer: a grant worker shares the supervisor's filesystem, process table and network stack, and only the base layers stand between it and them. Under the namespace sandbox a flaw in one base layer still leaves the grant worker in empty namespaces. Under the filter sandbox it does not.

The Gateway never switches sandboxes on its own. Startup runs a grant worker under the sandbox you chose and logs what it applied:

Gateway worker sandbox "namespaces": namespaces, non-dumpable, Landlock ABI v7, seccomp allow-list

When the sandbox cannot start, the Gateway exits with the sandbox, the layer that failed and the cause, and serves nothing:

worker sandbox "namespaces" failed: namespaces: bwrap: No permissions to create new namespace

The layer is namespaces when bubblewrap could not run or the host refused its namespaces, launch when the filter sandbox could not start the grant worker, and otherwise the base layer that failed: non-dumpable, Landlock or seccomp allow-list. First try to fix what the host refused, using the troubleshooting table. Change worker_sandbox only after reading the trade-off above. ADR 0001 records the decision and its evidence.

docs.title: Start the Broker and issue credentials
docs.text:
Create a service-owned SQLite state directory and private files for the backend token and Workload HMAC key. For shared mode add a Gateway service token. Provision an independent administrator token to enable stop and recovery operations. Keep each secret at least 32 bytes long and distinct. Put only public client-certificate trust anchors in client_ca_file.

Start countersign-broker broker.json. Serve the Integrator site and its theme manifest over HTTPS at the verified origin. Route /v1/companion to the Broker with WebSocket upgrades and subprotocol countersign.v1. Keep backend, Gateway and admin routes on the appropriate service ingress. The Broker can terminate TLS itself or listen on loopback behind HTTPS ingress. The Gateway always verifies TLS to its configured Broker URL. Integrator setup · Broker settings

The authenticated Integrator backend derives the user, Context and Workload instance, then calls POST /v1/backend/workloads with its backend credential. The Broker returns a token, binding and absolute expiry. Tokens last 120 seconds. For a sidecar, atomically replace the private token file before expiry with a token for the same binding and generation. The demo refreshes it every 60 seconds. In shared mode a CONNECT uses its original bearer token for subsequent Broker calls. Present a fresh token on a new CONNECT before continuing with an expiring credential. A higher generation retires the former instance. When a job finishes, the backend can retire its exact binding with /v1/backend/workloads/retire.

docs.title: Set destinations and approval scope
docs.text:
Configure matching rule IDs, versions, patterns and approval scopes at the Broker and Gateway. An exact rule wins over a wildcard. For example, *.corp.example:443 matches api.corp.example:443 only one label below the suffix. The apex, deeper names and other ports require their own entries. By default the prompt covers only the exact host. To offer approval across the wildcard, set whole_wildcard: true at the Broker and approval: "whole_wildcard" at the Gateway. Each intercepted host still receives its own leaf.

For an internal site, specify its exact DNS name and port and put its allowed addresses in private_networks. The parent validates the entire DNS answer set, including IPv4-mapped IPv6, before pinning one socket address. A mixed allowed/forbidden answer fails the connection. Add site-specific infrastructure and control-plane ranges to denied_networks. The Gateway also rejects special-use addresses including loopback, link-local, shared carrier space and known metadata endpoints. Within TLS it checks SNI and the authority of each HTTP request. Destination fields

docs.title: Maintain trust and stop access
docs.text:
Broker client trust determines which native certificate can represent a user. Gateway destination trust determines which server can receive a signature for a handshake. Supply signed DER CRLs or OCSP responses on the appropriate side when strict status checking is required. Arrange an external importer to verify its data source and atomically replace the files before expiry. Use a directory mount so file replacement is visible. A missing, stale or revoked result denies use. The Gateway rereads upstream roots and status during each handshake and at ten-second revalidation intervals. A shortened validity deadline cuts off idle connections as well as active traffic. Status evidence formats

Use a controlled cutover for changes to destination policy, issuer credentials or trust anchors.

  1. Stop new protected jobs. Use an authenticated admin POST to /v1/admin/control. {"operation":"issuer","stopped":true} withdraws pending and approved authority across this Broker. {"operation":"emergency","stopped":true} stops access across the Integrator. For a narrower response use {"operation":"destination","user":"USER","entry":"ENTRY","denied":true} or {"operation":"account","user":"USER","blocked":true}.
  2. Allow time for existing leases to expire, or stop affected Gateway processes to close their sockets. The Gateway watches for retirements and enforces independent ingress and egress leases with a 30-second maximum budget. A stop reported by the Broker records intent. Socket-closure observations identify connections on which the Gateway actually reported cutoff.
  3. Replace files, bump changed destination rule versions at both services and restart affected processes. Recreate sidecars to generate a fresh constrained CA. For shared issuers, distribute the corresponding public trust to Workloads and verify the expected issuer, chain and exact SAN in a test connection.
  4. Clear the same admin control with its boolean set to false, mint fresh Workload tokens and have users approve new work. Clearing a stop permits new grants. Earlier revoked grants remain terminal.

docs.title: Back up and recover the Broker
docs.text:
One Broker owns a database at a time. The database records the Integrator ID and verified origin and uses an adjacent lock file. Protect the state directory, backups, service credentials and status imports. Take a consistent SQLite backup into a private backup directory.

umask 077
sqlite3 /state/broker.db ".backup '/backup/broker.db'"

Stop the Broker before restoring the snapshot. Restore it under the owning service account with the same Integrator ID and verified origin. Run recovery to completion before starting the listener.

countersign-broker --recover-backup /config/broker.json
countersign-broker /config/broker.json

Recovery fences saved authority, removes saved enrollment and push subscriptions, retires saved Workload bindings and sets emergency stop. Review access changes since the snapshot, reestablish pairings and subscriptions, and use fresh Workload identities or higher generations. Clear emergency stop when ready to admit new approvals. Choose a new Context ID if the restored one is closed. An ordinary Broker restart cancels pending and approved grants and invalidates the previous boot's Workload tokens. Its device enrollments survive.

docs.title: Audit and troubleshoot
docs.text:
Use the backend's authenticated POST /v1/backend/status with the server-derived user and approval ID. Read the decision state, current ready, historical upstream_mtls_accepted, and reported ingress/egress closure counts separately. The Gateway records acceptance after it receives an HTTP response from the authenticated site. A site can return an HTTP error over an accepted mTLS connection.

Operators with authorized database access can inspect approval events without exporting private credential or subscription records. The default audit retention is 30 days. Ownership, status and control APIs

sqlite3 -readonly /state/broker.db \
  "SELECT datetime(occurred_at,'unixepoch'), approval, kind FROM audit ORDER BY occurred_at DESC LIMIT 20;"
Symptom Where to look Gateway exits with worker sandbox "<sandbox>" failed: <layer>: <cause> Run under the intended service UID, and verify the packaged Gateway rather than testing as root. The layer says what the host refused. Under "namespaces", layer namespaces: check that /usr/bin/bwrap exists, the host's user namespace policy, the library mounts and the container's seccomp and AppArmor profile. Under "filter", layer launch: check that the Gateway can run its own executable. Under either, layer non-dumpable, Landlock or seccomp allow-list: the container security profile refuses a call the grant worker confines itself with, or the kernel lacks seccomp filters. A host that cannot create namespaces at all needs a deliberate choice: read Choose a worker sandbox. CONNECT returns 407 Shared clients need an HTTPS proxy and one proxy bearer header. Check the token audience, expiry, broker boot, and separate service credential. CONNECT returns 403 or keeps asking for approval Compare rule ID, version, port, grant scope, memberships and stop controls. A denied or expired prompt requires an explicit retry. Check that the Companion is paired, online and can access the selected identity. CONNECT returns 429, 503 or 504 Inspect limits per grant/user, Broker availability, worker fencing, clock synchronization and pending approval. Capture the safe Countersign-Error and Countersign-Request-ID response headers for correlation. CONNECT succeeds, then TLS closes Check the Workload's current public proxy CA, exact hostname/SNI, server roots/status, issuer profile, client-certificate request and native provider. Check the owned status before treating a TLS failure as an application response. A long session closes Check grant, certificate, status and token deadlines, lease renewal, host clock drift and revocation. Closing the Companion prevents new signatures. An established connection continues while its remote authority remains valid.

docs.title: Try Countersign with curl
docs.text: In this walkthrough, curl runs in a container and calls https://site.test:9444/. The site requires a client certificate. The desktop holds the candidate identities. You can verify exactly which certificate the site received, then revoke the grant and try the same request again.

docs.title: Start the local demo
docs.text:
Use a Linux desktop session and a regular user with Docker Compose access. Have the packaged Linux Companion or an unpacked build available. The launcher uses D-Bus, GNOME Keyring, libsecret tools, SoftHSM2, Chromium, and Python. On Ubuntu 24.04 the desktop prerequisites include dbus-daemon, gnome-keyring, libsecret-tools, softhsm2, libnss3-tools, apparmor-utils, and python3-venv.

Run from the repository root:

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r examples/demo-integrator/test/fixture-requirements.txt
.venv/bin/python -m playwright install chromium
.venv/bin/python examples/demo-integrator/compose_demo.py \
  --app /absolute/path/to/countersign-companion

Replace the app path with your executable. If you have Chromium installed, you can skip the Playwright browser download and pass --browser /absolute/path/to/chromium. The launcher creates a disposable token, keyring, browser profile, and Companion profile. It builds the service images and prints the Integrator origin and the path to a temporary login secret. On Ubuntu hosts that restrict user namespaces, it requests sudo to load a temporary AppArmor profile for the demo and removes it on exit.

docs.title: Pair the desktop
docs.text:
The screenshots below are rendered from fixtures with the example names from Add Countersign to a service: origin https://portal.example, account u-42 and host ledger.partner.example:443. Your run shows the printed https://localhost origin, demo-user and site.test:9444.

  1. Open the Companion’s Integrators tab. Enter the printed HTTPS origin in Integrator origin and choose Pair. The Companion shows a pairing code.
  2. In the browser tab opened by the Companion, sign in with the temporary secret from the printed file. Enter the pairing code shown in the Companion and choose Confirm pairing.

  1. In the Companion, check that the origin and account belong to this demo and that the code matches the browser. Choose Confirm pairing. The Integrator appears in the list with Connected.

docs.title: Choose a certificate and verify it
docs.text:
Type curl at the launcher's prompt. The Workload already has the proxy address and the public sidecar CA. The first request waits while you decide, and the Companion opens its Requests tab.

Read Integrator, Account, Context, Requested host and Approval covers under Checked by Countersign. Choose one certificate, note its SHA-256 fingerprint, pick a duration, check Access ends, and choose Approve. The site obtains the certificate from the authenticated TLS connection and returns its fingerprint. A capture from the demo returned:

{"fingerprint":"c64a4b8b8bcdac1a7ac2bedcd13c520f4abfc07d5765d68df67f56ed0058f00b","subject":"Demo user"}

Each launch creates fresh certificates. Compare the response to the fingerprint you selected in your run. Matching subject names alone cannot identify the key that signed the handshake. The launcher also hands the result to the Integrator: open Job result on the demo page. It compares the fingerprint the site received with the certificate you approved, which the Integrator reads from the Broker's approval status.

docs.title: End access
docs.text:
In the Companion, open Integrators, choose the demo Integrator and choose Revoke access under the approval. Wait for Broker recorded revocation, then type curl again. A new connection from that Workload should fail. An explicit Request access from the Integrator starts a fresh approval. Type quit at the launcher prompt to remove the demo containers and disposable local state.

If the request stalls, first look for Connected in the Companion, then for a pending request on the Requests tab. An empty certificate list points to desktop identity discovery. A request that fails after approval needs a check of upstream trust and certificate acceptance. Companion troubleshooting · Integrator troubleshooting

docs.title: Broker HTTP API
docs.text:
The Integrator's backend authenticates users, checks Context ownership and selects the Workload and destination. Call the Broker over HTTPS with Content-Type: application/json and exactly one Authorization: Bearer <credential> header. The backend routes take plain JSON objects. The Gateway routes take versioned protocol frames. Integration walkthrough · Wire protocol

Caller Credential Routes Integrator backend Secret from backend_token_file POST /v1/backend/* Integrator administrator Separate secret from admin_token_file POST /v1/admin/control Sidecar Gateway Short-lived Workload token with audience countersign:broker:workload POST /v1/gateway/* Shared Gateway Workload token with audience countersign:gateway:workload, plus its own X-Countersign-Gateway service credential POST /v1/gateway/* Companion Fresh pairing-key proof on its outbound WebSocket GET /v1/companion upgrade, subprotocol countersign.v1

Both Gateway modes send a stable boot UUID in X-Countersign-Gateway-Instance. Keep all backend, administrator and Gateway service credentials out of browser responses. Credential verification

docs.title: Bind the Workload
docs.text:
POST /v1/backend/workloads HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <backend credential>

{"user":"u-42","context":"close-q3","workload":"export-981","workload_generation":1,"mode":"sidecar"}

The Broker returns HTTP 200 with the following shape. Token and timestamp values below are illustrative.

{
  "binding": {
    "integrator": "finance",
    "user": "u-42",
    "context": "close-q3",
    "workload": "export-981",
    "workload_generation": 1
  },
  "token": "<signed Workload JWT>",
  "expires_at_ms": 1794960120000
}

Reuse the entire returned binding in subsequent calls. mode defaults to sidecar. Shared mode requires a configured Gateway service credential. A token lasts 120 seconds. Reissue for the same live generation to refresh it. Replacing a Workload with a higher generation withdraws its old approvals. A retired generation cannot be reopened. Each Broker boot starts a fresh token epoch. Workload and approval handlers

docs.title: Backend operations
docs.text:
All paths in this table start with /v1/backend/ and use POST. A 204 response has an empty body. For renew, status and revoke, pass the approval ID returned by requests or renew.

Path JSON request fields Success pairings/confirm user, attempt from the pairing page URL, code entered by the user 204. The Companion can proceed to its own account confirmation and key proof. An incorrect code consumes the attempt. devices user 200 with {"devices":[…]}. Each item carries binding, connected, connected_at_ms and nullable observed_address. pairings/forget user, targets array of current device bindings 200 with the remaining devices. Removes the target pairings and withdraws their grants. requests binding, host such as ledger.partner.example:443 200 with {"id":"…","state":"pending"} or an existing matching approved record. An explicit request can retry a previously denied, cancelled or expired scope. status user, id 200 with the status and observations described below. approvals/current binding, host 200 with the status view of that Workload's current approval for the host: the one its Gateway traffic uses, including one the Workload's own connection started. 404 unavailable when it has none. Unlike requests, it never creates an approval. A pending renewal becomes current only once approved. renew binding, id of the live approved request 200 with the new pending approval ID. The previous grant remains usable until its deadline or a successful replacement. revoke user, id 204. Records withdrawal and cancels an outstanding renewal for that approval. Repeat calls for the same owned record are idempotent. workloads/retire binding 204. Retires that Workload generation. contexts/close user, context 204. Closes that user's Context and withdraws its pending and active approvals. push/subscribe user, subscription containing endpoint and keys (p256dh, auth) 204. Requires configured Web Push, valid subscription keys and an allowed HTTPS push host. push/unsubscribe user, endpoint 204. Removes the owner's subscription.

Take device bindings directly from a fresh devices response. Each contains pairing, key and channel_generation. Show the user the selected devices before calling pairings/forget. A reconnect changes the generation. If the snapshot is stale, refresh the list and confirm the selection again. Device and access controls · Web Push registration

docs.title: Read approval status
docs.text:
{
  "id": "85b80155-ac10-487f-a024-5216ec7f8ced",
  "state": "approved",
  "ready": true,
  "expires_at_ms": 1795470000000,
  "certificate": {
    "sha256": "c64a4b8b8bcdac1a7ac2bedcd13c520f4abfc07d5765d68df67f56ed0058f00b",
    "subject": "CN=Demo user",
    "issuer": "CN=Countersign demo client-ca",
    "not_after_ms": 1795635570000
  },
  "upstream_mtls_accepted": false,
  "ingress_closed_count": 0,
  "egress_closed_count": 0
}
  • state is pending, approved, denied, cancelled, expired or replaced. A pending offer has a ten-minute deadline. A successful renewal changes the predecessor's state to replaced.
  • ready means the winning Companion acknowledged activation and its matching channel is currently connected. An approved grant can have ready: false while that Companion is offline.
  • expires_at_ms and certificate describe the grant the user approved. They appear once an approval has a grant, and stay after it ends (expired, cancelled or replaced); a renewal's successor has its own approval ID and its own values. They are absent when the approval never had a grant: it is pending, denied, or it was expired or cancelled before anyone approved it. They are also absent once the audit retention period removes an ended approval's grant record.
  • expires_at_ms is the deadline the user approved, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch, in whole seconds. It is not always when access ends: a revocation, a renewal or a Gateway lease can end it sooner, and state says whether the grant is still in force.
  • certificate.sha256 is the lowercase hex SHA-256 of the client certificate the user selected (its DER encoding). It is the fingerprint the Companion shows, without its spaces, of the certificate the protected site receives in the handshake.
  • certificate.subject and certificate.issuer are that certificate's distinguished names, written in the order the certificate encodes them and joined with , (often most general first, such as C=US, O=Acme, CN=Jane, the reverse of RFC 4514), and certificate.not_after_ms is its own expiry, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch. A grant recorded by a Broker older than these fields has sha256 alone. A matching subject does not identify the key; compare sha256.
  • upstream_mtls_accepted is historical. It becomes true after the Gateway reports receiving upstream HTTP response headers on an authenticated connection.
  • ingress_closed_count and egress_closed_count count distinct reported socket closures on the two legs. Reports are best effort. Enforcers cut traffic at their local lease deadline even if they cannot report back. Gateway observations

docs.title: Administrator controls
docs.text:
POST /v1/admin/control returns 204. Each row is a complete example body. Changing the boolean to false clears that restriction. Previously withdrawn approvals require fresh consent.

Effect JSON body Block the account {"operation":"account","user":"u-42","blocked":true} Deny an account access to a configured destination entry {"operation":"destination","user":"u-42","entry":"ledger","denied":true} Stop issuer-dependent access across the Integrator {"operation":"issuer","stopped":true} Engage the Integrator emergency stop {"operation":"emergency","stopped":true}

docs.title: Handle failed calls
docs.text:
Broker application errors use a plain-text code. JSON decoding or request-size errors can also be returned by the HTTP layer.

HTTP Broker code Caller action 400 invalid_request Check the payload shape, exact host and variant for this endpoint. 401 unauthenticated Check the credential class, audience and expiry. Refresh a Workload token through the backend. 403 denied Recheck ownership, active generation, permission and device binding. 404 unavailable The referenced item is unavailable in this authenticated scope. For Push registration, also check whether a sender is configured. 409 already_resolved Fetch current status or a fresh device snapshot before acting again. 410 expired Refresh status. A user can explicitly request another approval. 429 busy Back off within the original request deadline. 503 authority_unavailable Restore Broker or storage availability.

The route table and error mapping are defined with the Broker HTTP service. HTTP error mapping and route registration

docs.title: Service configuration
docs.text: The Broker and Gateway take a JSON file as a positional argument. Paths in the file are local to the process, including its container mount namespace. Use absolute paths. Unknown fields fail deserialization. The reference Broker uses one SQLite database per Integrator and verified origin. Operating guide · Integrator guide

docs.title: Commands and Workload environment
docs.text:
Command Effect countersign-broker /config/broker.json Opens the database, starts a new authority epoch, applies configuration and listens. countersign-broker --recover-backup /config/broker.json Runs offline after a restore. Fences previous authority and leaves emergency stop enabled. countersign-gateway serve /config/gateway.json Probes the chosen worker sandbox and exits if it cannot start, opens the configured issuer, publishes the sidecar public CA when applicable, and listens. countersign-gateway env /config/gateway.json Writes shell-quoted exports using proxy_url and ca_output. The launcher supplies these values to the Workload.

For the sidecar configuration on this page, the helper exports these four values.

export HTTPS_PROXY='http://gateway:8080'
export SSL_CERT_FILE='/trust/sidecar.pem'
export REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE='/trust/sidecar.pem'
export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS='/trust/sidecar.pem'

Configure proxy use in the HTTP client or adapter the Workload runs. Clear any NO_PROXY bypass for the protected site. The Compose curl Workload also sets CURL_CA_BUNDLE to that public PEM. With an HTTPS shared proxy, configure the client to trust the listener certificate as well as the intercepted site's proxy leaf, for example with curl's --proxy-cacert and --cacert respectively.

docs.title: Broker
docs.text:
This example uses the demo's destination, service names and mounted paths. The reference launcher substitutes the configured desktop-facing port for 8443. Each executable runs in its own container. Demo configuration generator

{
  "origin": "localhost:8443",
  "listen": "0.0.0.0:9443",
  "integrator": "demo",
  "database": "/state/broker.db",
  "backend_token_file": "/config/backend.token",
  "workload_hmac_key_file": "/config/workload.hmac",
  "client_ca_file": "/config/client-ca.pem",
  "tls": {
    "certificate_path": "/config/broker.pem",
    "key_path": "/config/broker.key"
  },
  "destinations": [
    {"id": "demo-site", "version": 1, "pattern": "site.test:9444"}
  ]
}
Field Required or default Meaning origin Required Verified Integrator DNS authority in host:port form. An omitted port means 443. Use the origin the user pairs with. listen Required Listener IP address and port. A plain HTTP listener must be loopback, behind Integrator HTTPS ingress. integrator Required Stable opaque Integrator ID. The database records this ID and origin. database Required SQLite file. The Broker needs write access to its directory for the database and sibling lock file. backend_token_file Required Private text bearer secret shared by the Broker and the authenticated Integrator backend. workload_hmac_key_file Required Private raw bytes used to derive the boot-specific HS256 signing key. gateway_token_file Optional Separate text service secret required for shared-mode Gateway authentication. admin_token_file Optional Separate text service secret for POST /v1/admin/control. Set it to operate or clear stops. client_ca_file Required Default PEM trust anchors for native client chains. Per-entry client_trust.ca_file overrides the path. destinations Required Array of Broker destination entries. Fields are listed below. max_duration_s 28800 Positive maximum approval duration in seconds. The suggested duration is the smaller of one hour and this maximum. audit_retention_days 30 Positive retention in days for audit and security history. tls Optional Object with required certificate_path (PEM listener chain) and key_path (PEM private key). Required for a non-loopback bind. web_push Optional Enables ID-only offline notifications. Set vapid_key_file to a private unpadded base64url 32-byte P-256 scalar, contact to a mailto: URI and allowed_hosts to a nonempty list of exact push-service domains.

Use independent random values for the HMAC key and each bearer secret. The service enforces a 32-byte minimum and rejects reused values. Keep the token files readable only by the services that use them. These commands create the required secrets in a new, private Broker configuration directory.

umask 077
openssl rand -hex 32 > backend.token
openssl rand 32 > workload.hmac

docs.title: Gateway
docs.text:
This sidecar example assumes the Gateway's private Workload-facing address is 172.22.0.2 and the site resolves to 172.23.0.4. Use the actual interface address and site prefix for your network. The Compose launcher discovers both. The workload object matches the binding returned by the demo Integrator's authenticated backend call.

{
  "listen": "172.22.0.2:8080",
  "proxy_url": "http://gateway:8080",
  "ca_output": "/trust/sidecar.pem",
  "broker_url": "https://broker:9443",
  "broker_ca": "/config/ca.pem",
  "workload_token": "/credential/workload.jwt",
  "workload": {
    "integrator": "demo",
    "user": "demo-user",
    "context": "demo-context",
    "workload": "demo-curl",
    "workload_generation": 1
  },
  "destinations": [
    {
      "id": "demo-site",
      "version": 1,
      "pattern": "site.test:9444",
      "private_networks": ["172.23.0.4/32"],
      "roots": "/config/ca.pem"
    }
  ]
}
Field Required or default Meaning listen Required Listener IP address and port. Choose a private Workload endpoint in sidecar mode. proxy_url Required Workload-facing listener origin. Use http for sidecars and https for shared mode. broker_url Required HTTPS origin for the Broker. Both URL fields accept an origin with an optional port and root path. Credentials, query strings and fragments cause an error. broker_ca Required PEM anchors for the Broker's TLS listener or its HTTPS ingress. ca_output Required in both modes The sidecar writes its public CA here. Create the parent directory before startup. In shared mode supply the path of the public trust PEM you distribute. The helper uses this path in both modes. workload_token Sidecar only, required Private file containing the backend-issued Workload bearer token. The Gateway rereads it on Broker calls. workload Sidecar only, required Object containing integrator, user, context, workload IDs and a positive workload_generation. destinations Required Array of Gateway entries. A sidecar needs at least one to construct its CA constraints. denied_networks [] Additional IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs to block across destinations. clock_uncertainty_ms 1000 Allowed UTC difference from the Broker, in milliseconds, from 0 through 29999. The Gateway subtracts the margin from absolute deadlines and checks its local clock against monotonic elapsed time. worker_sandbox "namespaces" The worker sandbox for every grant worker, in sidecar and shared mode. "namespaces" is the namespace sandbox: bubblewrap gives each grant worker its own filesystem, process and network view, and the grant worker then confines itself with a seccomp allow-list, Landlock and non-dumpable memory. It needs /usr/bin/bwrap and a host that lets the Gateway create namespaces. "filter" is the filter sandbox: the same confinement without the namespaces, for a host that refuses them, such as ECS Fargate. It needs no bubblewrap. Any other value fails loading. The Gateway never switches from one to the other. Choose a worker sandbox shared Omitted → sidecar Shared-mode object. Requires PEM listener_cert and listener_key, a gateway_token file holding the Broker's matching service secret, and a ca source below. Omit both sidecar Workload fields.

docs.title: Destination entries
docs.text:
Use a unique stable id, positive version, and unique pattern at both services. Patterns are DNS authorities with an optional port (default 443), e.g. api.example.org:443 or *.example.org:443. The wildcard consumes one whole leftmost label. Exact entries take precedence. A downstream CONNECT requires an explicit port.

Field Process Default and purpose whole_wildcard Broker false. Set to true on a wildcard entry to offer a grant for the wildcard scope. client_trust Broker Optional object. ca_file selects alternative PEM client roots. user_fingerprints maps user IDs to allowed leaf SHA-256 fingerprints (standard padded base64 of 32 bytes). Omission permits identities passing the other checks. A supplied map requires a match for that user. revocation configures status imports. approval Gateway "exact_host". Set to "whole_wildcard" only for a wildcard with the corresponding Broker setting. private_networks Gateway []. For an exact private destination, list allowed CIDRs.
